label: Strongly improving
rationale: Cost to LEO has fallen ~40× from the Space Shuttle era ($54,500/kg) to $1,500/kg for Falcon Heavy. With Starship operational, another 10–100× reduction is possible by 2030.

label: Distant — currently at 3.1%
rationale: Annual mass to orbit reached a record 3,141 tonnes in 2025, ~3% of the 100,000-tonne threshold. Reaching it requires ~1,000 Starship-class flights per year; at current ~20–40% growth it would take 15–20 years, with the earliest plausible date in the early 2030s.

label: Distant — targeting mid-2030s
rationale: No crewed lunar landing has occurred since 1972; Starship HLS delays push the first Artemis crewed landing to ~2028, and a permanent base is realistic only by the mid-2030s. ISRU remains unproven on planetary surfaces, as VIPER's cancellation and revival illustrate.

label: Approaching — first products expected 2026–2027

label: Progressing: no recurring space-made product sold yet; drug-making flight due early 2027; ETA ~2036
rationale: No space-made product is yet sold on Earth from repeated production, and none of today's ventures has reported even a first sale to customers who use its product. label: Distant: no crewed landing since 1972; space-grown food still experimental; ETA ~2069
rationale: Space stations already recycle nearly all their water, and China's all its oxygen, but none grows a meaningful share of its crew's food, and a largely self-sufficient year has been shown only in a ground test; the first crewed Moon landing since 1972 is planned for 2028 and NASA's permanent outpost from 2032. Allowing for a landing, then a permanent base, then a decision to grow the base's own food and a decade to achieve it gives a 68% chance by 2100 and a median of 2069 (10% chance by 2044), so red. Whether anyone commits to growing a base's own food is the main uncertainty: funded requirements for it at both the US and Chinese bases would pull the median into the late 2050s.

label: Stalled: $1,673/kg (2025, Falcon Heavy), flat since 2021 vs its own long-run fall of 2.4%/yr
rationale: The cheapest ride to orbit in 2025 was still Falcon Heavy, whose last published list price (2022) works out to $1,673/kg in 2025 dollars; no rocket in service published a cheaper price through 2025, so the price has been flat since 2021 after falling 19% a year over 2016–2020. Across its whole record since 1962 the cheapest price has fallen 2.4% a year on average; five flat years against that decline make the status red. Prices published in 2026 do not break the stall: Falcon 9's list price rose to $74M ($3,364/kg, not inflation-adjusted) and SpaceX's rideshare price rose too. What could change it: Starship, which first reached orbit with a payload in September 2026, has one disclosed launch price so far, $90M for the Starlab station, about $900/kg at its 100-tonne design capacity; if it counts as a rocket in service with a published price, that would roughly halve the cheapest price.

label: Inching: China's station recycles all its oxygen, 96% of its water; food still comes from Earth
rationale: In September 2026 China said the recycling system on its Tiangong station had run for more than five years regenerating all of its oxygen and over 96% of its water, and wheat grown there had completed a full cycle with a second crop from its seeds near harvest; in April NASA reported that its brine processor, the step that took the ISS's water recovery to 98% in 2023, had run for about three years. Next, NASA's waste-recycling trailer feeding a garden is being tested with people in a North Dakota mock habitat through September 2028.

label: Inching: a lab rig made oxygen at ~1.7 kg a day from simulated moon soil; no real ice dug up yet
rationale: In July 2026 NASA published the oxygen output of a late-2024 ground test in which 25 kg of simulated lunar soil, melted and electrolysed in vacuum, gave oxygen at a rate of about 1.7 kg a day, and in February a reactor driven by concentrated sunlight took simulated soil as far as carbon monoxide, the step before oxygen; both are lab rigs, nowhere near production scale. Nothing has yet dug up or processed real lunar ice: the 2025 drill attempt failed when its lander tipped over, China's Chang'e-7 resource survey missed its August 2026 launch and slipped to 2027 at the earliest, and a lunar orbiter camera found less ice on the surface of shadowed craters than predicted, though radar hints at ice buried below. NASA's VIPER rover, due to launch in late 2027, and a lander payload to extract helium-3 from lunar soil, ready for 2028, are the next direct tests on the Moon.

label: Advancing: vest flown on Artemis I would cut solar-storm dose 40-60%; cosmic rays still pass
rationale: In August 2026 a peer-reviewed analysis of the mannequin experiment flown around the Moon on Artemis I found that a 26 kg wearable vest would cut the dose from a severe solar storm by roughly 40-60%, the first test of wearable protection beyond Earth orbit, though the storm figures are extrapolated from the belt radiation the mannequins actually met; in April the Artemis II crew returned from their ten-day lunar flyby with the first crew dose measured beyond Earth orbit since Apollo, about 10 mGy, most of it from Earth's radiation belts. Galactic cosmic rays still pass through any practical shielding: a study of measured doses found that a slow Mars trip stays under NASA's career limit only if flown near solar maximum or on a faster trajectory. Europe's first cosmic-ray simulator, opened in March in Darmstadt, adds a second facility for testing shielding against them.

advances.what: Science Advances (DLR-led MARE, flown on Artemis I): first evaluation of wearable shielding in deep space; the ~26 kg HDPE AstroRad vest would cut effective dose by ~58% in an August-1972-like and ~40% in an October-1989-like solar particle event (up to 193 and 131 days of deep-space exposure spared).
